99942 Apophis.title: 99942 Apophis
99942 Apophis.extract: 99942 Apophis (provisional designation 2004 MN4) is a near-Earth asteroid classified as a potentially hazardous object. Its mean diameter is about 340–370 metres (1,120–1,210 ft), while radar observations indicate an elongated shape with a long axis of about 450 metres (1,480 ft) and suggest that it may be bilobed. It was discovered on 19 June 2004 by Roy A. Tucker, David J. Tholen, and Fabrizio Bernardi at Kitt Peak National Observatory. The asteroid was numbered 99942 in 2005 and named after Apophis, the Greek name of the ancient Egyptian serpent deity Apep.

101955 Bennu.title: 101955 Bennu
101955 Bennu.extract: 101955 Bennu (provisional designation 1999 RQ36) is a carbonaceous asteroid in the Apollo group, discovered by the LINEAR Project on 11 September 1999. It is a potentially hazardous object that is listed on the Sentry Risk Table and has the second highest cumulative rating on the Palermo scale. It has a cumulative chance of around 1 in 1,750 of impacting Earth between 2178 and 2290 with the greatest risk being on 24 September 2182. It is named after Bennu, the ancient Egyptian mythological bird associated with the Sun, creation, and rebirth.

162173 Ryugu.title: 162173 Ryugu
162173 Ryugu.extract: 162173 Ryugu (provisional designation 1999 JU3) is a near-Earth object and also a potentially hazardous asteroid of the Apollo group. It measures approximately 900 metres (3,000 ft) in diameter and is a dark object of the rare spectral type Cb, with qualities of both a C-type asteroid and a B-type asteroid. In June 2018, the Japanese spacecraft Hayabusa2 arrived at the asteroid. After making measurements and taking samples, Hayabusa2 left Ryugu for Earth in November 2019 and returned the sample capsule to Earth on 5 December 2020. The samples showed the presence of organic compounds, such as uracil (one of the four components in RNA) and vitamin B3.

65803 Didymos.title: 65803 Didymos
65803 Didymos.extract: 65803 Didymos is a sub-kilometer asteroid and binary system that is classified as a potentially hazardous asteroid and near-Earth object of the Apollo group. The asteroid was discovered in 1996 by the Spacewatch survey at Kitt Peak, and its small 160-meter minor-planet moon, named Dimorphos, was discovered in 2003. Due to its binary nature, the asteroid was then named Didymos, the Greek word for 'twin'.

2024 YR4.title: 2024 YR4
2024 YR4.extract: 2024 YR4 is an asteroid with an estimated diameter of 53 to 67 metres (174 to 220 ft) that is classified as an Apollo-type (Earth-crossing) near-Earth object. 25143 Itokawa.title: 25143 Itokawa
25143 Itokawa.extract: 25143 Itokawa (provisional designation 1998 SF36) is a sub-kilometer near-Earth object of the Apollo group and also a potentially hazardous asteroid. It was discovered by the LINEAR program in 1998 and later named after Japanese rocket engineer Hideo Itokawa. The peanut-shaped S-type asteroid has a rotation period of 12.1 hours and measures approximately 330 meters (1,100 feet) in diameter. Due to its low density and high porosity, Itokawa is considered to be a rubble pile, consisting of numerous boulders of different sizes rather than of a single solid body.

1 Ceres.title: Ceres (dwarf planet)
1 Ceres.extract: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. It was the first object identified in the asteroid belt, discovered on 1 January 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi at Palermo Astronomical Observatory in Sicily, and announced as a new planet. Ceres was later classified as an asteroid, and then more recently as the only confirmed dwarf planet within the asteroid belt, and the largest without a moon. It is also the only recognized dwarf planet in the solar system whose orbit lies within that of Neptune. In the minor planet numbering system, its designation is 1 Ceres or (1) Ceres.

3200 Phaethon.title: 3200 Phaethon
3200 Phaethon.extract: 3200 Phaethon, provisionally designated 1983 TB and previously sometimes erroneously spelled Phæton, is an active Apollo asteroid with an orbit that brings it closer to the Sun than any other named asteroid. For this reason, it was named after the Greek Hero, Phaëthon, son of the sun god Helios. It is 5.8 km (3.6 mi) in diameter and is the parent body of the Geminids meteor shower of mid-December. With an observation arc of 35+ years, it has a very well determined orbit. The 2017 Earth approach distance of about 10 million km was known with an accuracy of ±700 m.

\u02bbOumuamua.extract: 1I/ʻOumuamua is the first confirmed interstellar object detected passing through the Solar System. Formally designated 1I/2017 U1, it was discovered by Canadian physicist Robert Weryk using the Pan-STARRS telescope at Haleakalā Observatory, Hawaii, on 19 October 2017, approximately 40 days after it passed its closest point to the Sun on 9 September. When it was first observed, it was about 33 million km from Earth and already heading away from the Sun.

1979 XB.title: 1979 XB
1979 XB.extract: 1979 XB is a lost asteroid with a short observation arc of 3.9 days that cannot be recovered with targeted observations and awaits serendipitous survey observations. It is classified as a near-Earth object and potentially hazardous asteroid of the Apollo group and is estimated to be 660 meters in diameter. The unnumbered minor planet has a poorly constrained orbit and has not been observed in 46 years. It has been listed on the Sentry Risk Table since the list started in 2002. As of 11 February 2025, With a cumulative Palermo scale rating of −2.70, the poorly known orbit and assumed size place 1979 XB fourth on an unconstrained listing of the Sentry Risk Table.

2000 SG344.title: 2000 SG344
2000 SG344.extract: 2000 SG344 is a small Aten asteroid first observed in 2000. It is assumed to have a diameter of approximately 37 meters (120 feet) – or roughly twice that of the Chelyabinsk meteor – and an assumed mass of 7.1×107 kg (71,000 tonnes), but the size is only known within about a factor 2. As of February 2025, it is the largest object known to have a better than 1/1000 chance (0.1%) of impacting Earth and has the fifth highest cumulative Palermo scale rating at −2.77. The next good chance to observe the object will be in May 2028 when it passes 0.02 AU (3,000,000 km; 1,900,000 mi) from Earth.

2010 RF12.title: 2010 RF12
2010 RF12.extract: 2010 RF12 is a very small asteroid, classified as a near-Earth object of the Apollo group, that passed between Earth and the Moon on 8 September 2010, at 21:12 UTC, approaching Earth within 79,000 kilometres (49,000 mi) above Antarctica. The asteroid was discovered by the Mount Lemmon Survey near Tucson, Arizona on 5 September 2010 along with 2010 RX30. Based on a short 7-day observation arc from that apparation, it was listed for 12 years on the Sentry Risk Table as the asteroid with the greatest known probability (5%) of impacting Earth. 2010 RF12 was rediscovered in August 2022, and now has a 12-year observation arc and a much better known orbit. As of the December 2022 solution which accounts for nongravitational forces, there is a 1-in-10 chance of an Earth impact on 5 September 2095.

2007 FT3.title: 2007 FT3
2007 FT3.extract: 2007 FT3 is a lost asteroid with a short observation arc of 1.2 days that cannot be recovered with targeted observations and awaits serendipitous survey observations. It has a poorly constrained orbit and has not been seen since 2007. It was first observed on 20 March 2007 when the asteroid was estimated to be 0.19 ± 0.01 astronomical units (28.4 ± 1.5 million kilometres) from Earth and had a solar elongation of 107 degrees. 2007 FT3 is the fourth largest asteroid with better than a 1-in-2 million cumulative chance of impacting Earth after (29075) 1950 DA, 1979 XB, and 101955 Bennu. With a cumulative Palermo Technical Impact Hazard Scale of –3.06, the poorly known orbit and assumed size place 2007 FT3 eighth on an unconstrained listing of the Sentry Risk Table.

2022 PX1.title: List of asteroid close approaches to Earth in 2022
2022 PX1.extract: Below is the list of asteroids that have come close to Earth in 2022.

items.name: TESS
items.what: Watches one big strip of sky for about 27 days at a time, looking for the tiny dip when a planet crosses its star.
items.here: Every star this lab searches comes from TESS.
items.counts: about 200,000 bright stars watched closely, millions more in its wide pictures

items.name: CHEOPS
items.what: Looks at one star with a known planet at a time, to measure the planet's size precisely.
items.here: Its public measurements are an answer key: a way to test a transit search on stars where the truth is known.
items.counts: a few hundred stars, one at a time

items.name: James Webb
items.what: Reads the air of distant planets from the starlight that passes through it.
items.here: The best small candidates around nearby red stars are the kind Webb could study next.
items.counts: a few dozen planets a year, in great detail

items.name: Gaia
items.what: Measured the positions and motions of nearly two billion stars. Release 4 covers five and a half years of measurements and should reveal stars that wobble because unseen planets tug on them.
items.here: This lab already uses Gaia to flag candidates whose star may have a hidden companion.

items.name: Euclid
items.what: Maps the shapes and distances of more than a billion galaxies to trace dark matter and dark energy. The first big release opens about 1,900 square degrees, one seventh of the planned survey; the complete first release follows in mid-2027.
items.here: Not planets: the widest view there is. Its deep-field pictures are a layer in the Space atlas.

items.name: Nancy Grace Roman
items.status: launched 30 August 2026, getting ready for science
items.what: Pictures as sharp as Hubble's but a hundred times wider. It will find planets when their gravity briefly magnifies a star behind them, and map dark energy.
items.here: Finds the cold planets far from their stars that TESS cannot see.
items.counts: hundreds of millions of stars toward the centre of our galaxy

items.name: PLATO
items.what: Twenty-six cameras watching at least 200,000 Sun-like stars for years, to find Earth-sized planets with year-long orbits.
items.here: The successor to TESS for a lab like this one: the same kind of brightness records, longer and more precise.

items.name: Vera C. Rubin Observatory
items.what: Photographs the whole southern sky every few nights for ten years: a film of everything that moves or changes.
items.here: Expected to discover millions of asteroids, each needing the kind of archive follow-up this lab does.
items.counts: billions of stars and galaxies, millions of asteroids

universe.blueshift_note: It is moving towards us, so its light is blueshifted, not redshifted. A redshift only gives a distance when the expansion of the universe carries a galaxy away, and the catalogue used here has no measured distance precise enough for it, so the map cannot place it. Almost every galaxy like this is one of the Milky Way's closest neighbours, right next to Home.
universe.method: Redshift corrected for our own motion and for infall towards Virgo, the Great Attractor and Shapley (Mould et al. 2000) below 3500 km/s, CMB frame above 7000 km/s, blended between; group members share the group mean velocity (Tully 2015); comoving distance with H0 = 70, matter 0.3. Cosmicflows-4 measured distances replace it within 45 Mpc when more precise. Environment: T-web of the selection-weighted density, 5 Mpc smoothing, eigenvalue threshold 0.7 on galaxy density (about 0.45 on matter).
universe.near_note: The survey measures almost no speed away from us for it. So close to home a galaxy's own motion matters more than the expansion of the universe, so its redshift cannot give a distance, and the catalogue used here has no measured distance precise enough for it. It is left out; it sits in or just outside the Local Group, right next to Home.

daily.blurb: This candidate signal shows a consistent drop in brightness every 14.5 days, which could be caused by a large object passing in front of its star. To decide if this is a planet, look at the light curve plots to see if the dips are deep, sharp, and repeat at the same time interval. If the dips look consistent and not like random noise, it could be a much larger world than Earth!

items.title: NASA’s ESCAPADE Completes Powered Earth Flybys, Now En Route to Mars
items.why: This marks a successful critical maneuver in a mission to reach Mars.
items.summary: Two ESCAPADE spacecraft successfully completed powered flybys of Earth. They used Earth's gravity and engine burns to help them travel toward Mars.

items.title: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, making a 10-year time-lapse of the night sky
items.why: This observatory will provide massive amounts of new data for many different areas of astronomy.
items.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory is using a ground-based telescope to create a 10-year time-lapse of the sky. This project will help scientists study dark matter, dark energy, and objects in our Solar System.

items.title: NASA unveils $10 billion in moon base contracts, new lunar missions and the 'PROMISE' of a nuclear-powered rover
items.why: This represents a massive step forward in human lunar exploration and infrastructure.
items.summary: NASA has announced $10 billion in contracts to help build a moon base by 2032. These plans include new lunar missions and a nuclear-powered rover.

items.title: JWST tracks more than 100 magnified stellar events in the Dragon galaxy
items.why: This massive increase in detections provides a significant new dataset for studying distant galaxies.
items.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope found 104 magnified stellar events in the Dragon galaxy. This is more than double the previous record of 44 events.

items.title: 'Stupendously large' primordial black holes ruled out as a dark matter source
items.why: This helps scientists narrow down what dark matter could actually be.
items.summary: Researchers have ruled out very large primordial black holes as a source of dark matter. These hypothetical black holes would have formed from dense matter in the early universe.

items.title: Science Release: Astronomers Discover Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the Oldest Compact Quasar Pair in the Universe
items.why: This discovery challenges our current understanding of how massive black holes formed in the early universe.
items.summary: Astronomers have found the oldest pair of compact quasars ever seen, located just 900 million years after the Big Bang. These two massive, feeding black holes are so large that scientists do not yet have a theory to explain how they grew so fast.

items.title: Gravitational waves hint at black holes born from failed supernovae
items.why: This provides evidence for a specific theory about how the universe's largest black holes are born.
items.summary: New evidence from gravitational waves suggests some black holes are created when massive stars fail to explode as supernovae. Instead of a big explosion, the star's core simply collapses into a black hole.

items.title: First Direct Measurement of Cosmic Hydrogen Could Change How We Map the Universe
items.why: This measurement provides a new way to understand the distribution of matter in the universe.
items.summary: Scientists have completed the first direct measurement of how cosmic hydrogen is clustered across the universe. This new data could change the way researchers map the large-scale structure of space.

items.title: NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
items.why: This research shows how a new space mission could help us discover new celestial objects using gravity.
items.summary: NASA scientists are studying how the future LISA observatory will use gravitational waves to find new worlds. These waves are tiny ripples in space-time caused by large objects orbiting each other.

items.title: A robot just built a structure autonomously in space for the 1st time ever
items.why: Autonomous assembly is a critical step for building massive structures in space far from Earth.
items.summary: A robot has successfully built a structure in space on its own for the first time. This technology could be used to assemble large telescopes or other equipment in orbit without humans.

items.title: Atmosphere of lava planet: ‘A cloudy, reflective sunscreen’
items.why: New data from the Webb telescope provides specific details about the atmosphere of a distant lava planet.
items.summary: The Webb telescope has observed a super-Earth called TOI-561 b, which is a planet covered in lava. The observations show that the planet has a very reflective and cloudy atmosphere.

items.title: Twin gas rings observed around a white dwarf
items.why: Finding these rings helps scientists understand how stars lose material and how white dwarfs behave.
items.summary: Astronomers have discovered two gas rings surrounding a white dwarf star. These rings are shaped like twins around the dead star.

items.title: The cold substellar frontier in JWST Extragalactic surveys: a robust parallax measurement yields the most distant known ultra-cold Y dwarf
items.why: This discovery helps astronomers map out the most distant and coldest objects in our neighborhood of the galaxy.
items.summary: Astronomers used the JWST to find a very cold, tiny object known as a Y dwarf. By measuring its movement over two years, they proved it is the most distant ultra-cold dwarf ever found.

items.title: The supernova impostor: Chandra finds likely source of giant star's repeated outbursts
items.why: It solves a mystery regarding the cause of extreme outbursts in massive stars.
items.summary: The Chandra X-ray Observatory has identified what causes a giant, unstable star to have repeated outbursts. This star is sometimes called a 'supernova impostor' because of its behavior.

items.title: Are the James Webb Space Telescope's mysterious Little Red Dots actually tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang era?
items.why: Identifying these objects could change our understanding of how the universe began and how black holes formed.
items.summary: Scientists are investigating small, red objects called Little Red Dots found by the James Webb Space Telescope. New research suggests these might actually be tiny black holes created during the Big Bang.

items.title: Theory predicting an older universe without dark matter or dark energy passes key cosmological tests
items.why: It challenges the standard model of how the universe began and functions.
items.summary: Researchers have proposed a new theory where the universe is 26.7 billion years old. This model suggests the universe does not need dark matter or dark energy to work.

items.title: Early Supermassive Black Holes Aren’t All Monsters
items.why: This helps astronomers understand how the largest objects in the universe first formed.
items.summary: Researchers searched for hidden supermassive black holes that existed in the early universe. The study suggests that these early black holes are not all as massive as previously thought.

items.title: Expanding the Volatile Abundance Inventory for High-Priority K-Dwarf JWST Exoplanet Systems
items.why: Knowing the chemical makeup of stars helps scientists understand the environments where planets form.
items.summary: Scientists studied the chemical makeup of six stars that have planets orbiting them. They measured how much carbon and oxygen these stars contain to help understand their planetary systems.

items.title: Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit
items.why: This research highlights the massive risks that space-based nuclear explosions pose to our global satellite infrastructure.
items.summary: Researchers studied what would happen to satellites in low Earth orbit if a nuclear weapon were detonated in space. They found that the radiation could disable almost all satellites in the area within one week.

items.title: Our sun's undiscovered stellar nemesis is still out there, says physicist
items.why: Understanding the potential for extinction-level comet impacts is vital for planetary defense.
items.summary: Physicists are discussing the possibility of dangerous comets that could cause mass extinctions on Earth. These comets are thought to come from a massive, spherical cloud of icy objects called the Oort cloud.

items.title: A Perseverance Experiment Could Help Astronauts Prepare for Dust Storms on Mars
items.why: Protecting astronauts from harsh environments like Martian dust storms is critical for successful human exploration.
items.summary: Scientists studied how Martian dust interacts with materials on the Perseverance Rover. This research helps planners understand how dust might affect future astronauts and their equipment on Mars.

items.title: Long-lived mineral grains can be invaluable for reconstructing impact events, but the stories are complex
items.why: Studying these minerals helps us reconstruct the history of how planets were formed and shaped.
items.summary: Scientists use long-lived mineral grains to study past impact events on Earth and the moon. These grains help researchers understand how the solar system and planets have changed over time.

items.title: Two nearby rocky worlds could offer alien astronomers views of planets appearing to reverse course
items.why: It provides insight into how life elsewhere might observe and study other planetary systems.
items.summary: Scientists are studying how two nearby rocky planets might look to alien astronomers. These planets could appear to move backward in their orbits from a different perspective.

items.title: Exploring Coronal Mass Ejections with Synthetic Spacecraft
items.why: Understanding how spacecraft interact with solar eruptions helps improve space weather forecasting.
items.summary: New research uses synthetic spacecraft to study how coronal mass ejections work. The study shows that the path a spacecraft takes changes how we understand these solar eruptions.

items.title: The Low-α Splash Population in the Milky Way
items.why: This research helps explain the early history and formation of our galaxy.
items.summary: Scientists are using models to study a specific group of stars in the Milky Way called the 'Splash' population. These stars have unique chemical properties and move in unusual orbits.

items.title: Hot gas in Cygnus
items.why: This provides interesting details about how stars interact with their environment.
items.summary: A nebula in the Cygnus constellation surrounds the Wolf-Rayet star WR 134. The star's strong winds are creating a bright bubble in the surrounding gas about 6,000 light-years away.

items.title: Mysterious gas on Mars suggests magma below
items.why: Finding active magma helps scientists understand if Mars is still geologically alive.
items.summary: Researchers found hydrogen chloride gas leaking from the ground near a large volcano on Mars. This discovery suggests that active magma might be buried underneath the surface.

items.title: A Stellar Odd Couple at an Unusual Stage of Evolution
items.why: Studying these objects helps us understand how stars live and die.
items.summary: Astronomers are studying a pair of stars where one is a millisecond pulsar and the other is becoming a white dwarf. The pulsar pulls material from its companion star, which speeds up the companion's evolution.

items.title: CHAPEA Mission 2 Crew Reflects After 378 Days on Simulated Mars
items.why: This research helps scientists understand how humans might survive long-term missions to Mars.
items.summary: Four volunteers have finished a 378-day simulation of living on Mars. They lived inside the Mars Dune Alpha habitat without windows or real-time contact with the outside world.

items.title: Sun news: Auroras continue! More tonight at northern U.S. latitudes?
items.why: Solar activity and solar wind speeds directly affect how much light shows up in our atmosphere as auroras.
items.summary: Fast solar winds reaching speeds over 800 km/s are causing solar storms. These storms may create auroras visible in the northern United States tonight.

items.title: ATel 18146: XMM-Newton detection of hard X-ray emission from the nearby Type Ia-CSM SN 2026sqf
items.why: Detecting X-rays from a nearby supernova helps scientists understand how these massive explosions work.
items.summary: Astronomers used the XMM-Newton telescope to detect X-rays from a nearby supernova called SN 2026sqf. This supernova is located in the galaxy NGC 3310.

items.title: Nearby Dwarf Galaxies Show Surprising Lack Of Oxygen, Says Paper
items.why: The lack of oxygen in these galaxies challenges current theories about galaxy evolution.
items.summary: A study of over 36 dwarf galaxies found they contain much less oxygen than expected. This finding suggests there are still things scientists do not understand about how galaxies grow.

items.title: Game theory helps SETI search for alien civilizations
items.why: New mathematical methods can make the search for extraterrestrial intelligence more efficient.
items.summary: Scientists are using game theory to improve the search for signs of alien civilizations. This method helps decide where to look for technosignatures from other intelligent life.

items.title: Backward world? Rubin finds a retrograde object past Neptune
items.why: Finding objects with unusual orbits helps us understand the history of our solar system.
items.summary: The Rubin Observatory found a new object orbiting the sun past Neptune. This object has a retrograde orbit, meaning it moves in a different direction than most planets.

items.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
items.why: This research helps scientists better identify signs of life on distant worlds.
items.summary: Astronomers are using computer models to simulate what a planet's atmosphere looks like if it has no life. This helps them tell the difference between empty rocky planets and those that might be inhabited.

items.title: A Mysterious Asteroid Is Accelerating in Space, And We're Running Out of Explanations
items.why: Understanding why an asteroid accelerates helps scientists learn more about how objects move in space.
items.summary: Scientists have observed a mysterious asteroid that is speeding up as it moves through space. Researchers are currently looking for explanations for what is causing this acceleration.

items.title: Earth's gravity may have kept the early moon's volcanic heart beating
items.why: It provides a new understanding of how the moon's internal heat and geology functioned in the past.
items.summary: New research suggests that Earth's gravity might have helped keep the early moon's volcanic center active. This challenges the idea that the moon cooled down very quickly after it formed.

items.title: A Stinky Gas Seeping From The Bowels of Mars May Reveal The Planet Is Still Volcanically Active
items.why: Knowing if Mars is volcanically active helps scientists understand if the planet could support life.
items.summary: Scientists have detected a smelly gas seeping from Mars. This could mean that the planet is still volcanically active.

items.title: Untangling the patterns of the cosmic microwave background to better understand the early universe
items.why: Understanding these patterns helps us learn about the very beginning of the universe.
items.summary: Scientists are studying patterns in the cosmic microwave background radiation. This helps them learn more about how the early universe formed.

items.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
items.why: This historical event provided early evidence of massive cosmic explosions.
items.summary: In 1572, a German astronomer saw a supernova using only his eyes. At the time, people thought they were seeing a brand new star.

items.title: A runaway star moves fast in an unusual direction
items.why: Studying runaway stars helps scientists understand the forces that can kick stars out of their normal paths.
items.summary: Most stars in our galaxy move together in an orderly way. This specific star is called a runaway star because it is moving very fast in an unusual direction.

items.title: Beyond the Fast Rotators: A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Substellar Weather
items.why: Studying a wide variety of objects helps scientists understand how weather works on different types of worlds.
items.summary: Scientists are planning a large study using the James Webb Space Telescope to study weather on brown dwarfs and giant planets. This project will look at many different objects instead of just one at a time.

items.title: Near-Ultraviolet and Optical Observations of the White Dwarf ZTF J0328$-$1219 Reveal Variable Periodicity in its Transiting Debris System
items.why: This helps us understand how debris disks around dead stars behave and change over time.
items.summary: Astronomers watched a white dwarf star that is surrounded by a ring of space debris. They noticed the debris moves in a changing pattern, which suggests pieces are crashing into each other.

items.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
items.why: Improving how we see faint planets makes it easier to find more worlds in the future.
items.summary: Researchers created a new mathematical method to remove the bright light of a star from an image. This allows them to see much fainter planets that were previously hidden by the star's glare.

items.title: Tracing the Epoch of Reionization through extreme emission line galaxies around Cosmic Noon
items.why: These specific galaxies act as markers to help us understand the history of the universe.
items.summary: Researchers studied a group of small, intense galaxies from a period called 'cosmic noon.' These galaxies are useful for studying how the early universe changed over time.

items.title: ATel 18151: Radio non-detection of nearby Type Ia SN 2026ahvu
items.why: Not detecting radio signals helps scientists understand the environment around a supernova explosion.
items.summary: Astronomers used the MeerKAT radio telescope to look for radio signals from a nearby supernova called SN 2026ahvu. They did not find any radio waves during their observation.

items.title: How the cosmic environment depletes galaxies of their gas
items.why: Understanding how galaxies lose gas helps scientists explain why some galaxies stop forming new stars.
items.summary: Researchers found out how dense areas of space can strip gas away from galaxies. They studied a group of galaxies located 7 billion light-years away to see this process in action.

items.title: Earth's 'core carbon' may have come from the far reaches of the solar system
items.why: It changes our understanding of how Earth's internal composition was created.
items.summary: Scientists believe much of the carbon inside Earth's core may have come from the far reaches of the solar system. This material likely arrived during the final stages of how the planets formed.

items.title: A distant exoplanet mysteriously vanished from sight. Astronomers just discovered why
items.why: Solving this helps astronomers better understand and track planets outside our solar system.
items.summary: Astronomers have figured out why a distant planet seemed to disappear after being watched for seven years. The mystery of its disappearance has now been solved.

items.title: ALMA Reveals a Jet of Cool Gas from a Microquasar
items.why: Studying these jets helps explain how energy is released by compact objects in space.
items.summary: The ALMA telescope has found a jet of cool gas coming from a microquasar in the Large Magellanic Cloud. This object is located inside the remains of an old supernova.

items.title: Uranus has a weird magnetic field that's stumped scientists for 40 years — we may finally know why
items.why: Solving this mystery helps explain how magnetic fields work inside giant planets.
items.summary: Scientists may have found the reason why Uranus has a strange, lopsided magnetic field. The field might be caused by extreme conditions inside the planet that increase electrical conductivity.

items.title: Why Aging Stars Suffer A Sudden Luminosity Dip
items.why: Understanding these brightness changes helps scientists model how stars evolve over time.
items.summary: As low-mass stars like our Sun get older, they move into a phase called the Red Giant Branch. During this time, their brightness usually goes up, but they experience a sudden dip known as the RGB luminosity bump.

items.title: X-ray observations uncover possible jet warning signs in black hole systems
items.why: Predicting these outbursts helps scientists understand the extreme physics of black hole environments.
items.summary: Scientists used X-ray observations to look for signs that a black hole might soon shoot out a jet of particles. These jets are powerful bursts of energy that help researchers understand how black holes work.

items.title: Simulations cast doubt on unusual asteroid's 'dark comet' status
items.why: Determining the true nature of the asteroid helps explain its unusual movement through space.
items.summary: New computer simulations are questioning if a strange asteroid is actually a 'dark comet.' Scientists are trying to explain why the small asteroid 1998 KY26 is accelerating unexpectedly.

items.title: Tiny Solar Whirlpools May Hold the Secret to the Sun’s Blistering Corona
items.why: Solving the heating mystery of the solar corona is a major goal in solar physics.
items.summary: New research suggests that tiny whirlpools in the Sun might explain why the outer atmosphere is so hot. This study helps solve the mystery of the temperature difference between the Sun's surface and its corona.

items.title: DMAJOR: A JWST Legacy Survey of Protoplanetary Disks
items.why: Mapping these disks helps us understand the physical conditions present during the birth of planetary systems.
items.summary: Scientists are proposing a new study using the James Webb Space Telescope to map the shapes of disks where planets form. This study will look at how dust, ice, and light are distributed in these environments.

items.title: Studying the Fullerene Nest: JWST Observations of the Planetary Nebula Tc 1. III. Tracing Fullerene-Linked Dust Variation
items.why: This research provides new details on how different types of cosmic dust and molecules are organized in planetary nebulae.
items.summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers studied a space cloud known as Tc 1 that contains fullerenes. They found that the dust in the cloud is distributed differently than the fullerenes.

items.title: ATel 18148: X-ray upper limit on the progenitor of the Type Ia supernova 2026ahvu in NGC 1433
items.why: Understanding what kind of star exploded helps scientists learn how different types of supernovae work.
items.summary: Astronomers looked at old X-ray data to see if they could find the star that exploded to create a recent supernova. They did not find any X-rays, which helps set a limit on how bright the original star was.

items.title: Constraining Dust Attenuation Curves in Star-Forming Galaxies at Cosmic Noon Using Multiple Emission Line Ratios
items.why: Knowing how dust affects light is essential for accurately measuring the properties of distant galaxies.
items.summary: Using the JWST telescope, researchers studied how dust blocks light in 386 distant galaxies. They found that the way dust affects light is different for every galaxy, even those that are at similar distances.

items.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5050-5055: It’s Nazca, Our 49th Drill Hole
items.why: Drilling helps scientists understand the mineral makeup of Mars and search for clues about its history.
items.summary: The Curiosity rover has completed its 49th drill hole, which scientists have named Nazca. The team is studying a specific area where they previously found unusual disc-shaped shapes in the rocks.

items.title: The ELT can probe ultra-diffuse galaxies and their dark matter mysteries
items.why: Understanding ultra-diffuse galaxies provides clues about how much dark matter exists in the universe.
items.summary: The upcoming Extremely Large Telescope will be powerful enough to study very faint, spread-out galaxies. This will help researchers learn more about the mysteries of dark matter.

items.title: Rubies on Mars?
items.why: Finding specific minerals helps scientists understand the history and chemistry of the Martian surface.
items.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has found evidence of minerals on Mars that look like rubies. These findings were made using the rover's specialized scientific instruments.

items.title: Subaru Telescope reveals the shape and temperature of Comet Encke's nucleus
items.why: Understanding the shape and temperature of a comet's nucleus provides insight into its composition.
items.summary: The Subaru Telescope has been used to study the nucleus of Comet Encke. Scientists discovered that the comet's core is elongated and measured its surface temperature.

items.title: First known 'disappearing planet' has a neighbor that makes it wobble like a top
items.why: This discovery helps scientists understand how planets move and interact with their neighbors.
items.summary: Astronomers found a gas giant planet that seems to disappear during observations. A nearby neighbor causes the planet to wobble as it orbits its star every 8.25 days.

items.title: Pakistani astronaut to board Shenzhou 24 and become the first foreigner on China's space station
items.why: It marks a significant moment for international cooperation on the Chinese space station.
items.summary: An astronaut from Pakistan is set to join the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft. This mission would make him the first foreign national to visit China's space station.

items.title: A TESS Disappearing Act: The Vanishing Transits of TOI-2535 b
items.why: This shows how gravity from other planets can change how we see a solar system.
items.summary: A large hot planet named TOI-2535 b is moving out of our view of its star. A nearby planet is pulling on it, causing its path to shift so it no longer crosses in front of the star.

items.title: Towards a new model of the compact triple system $λ$ Tauri I. Improved periods and preliminary elements of the triple system
items.summary: Researchers analyzed new and old data to create much more accurate timing models for the orbits in the triple star system λ Tauri. They found that one star in the inner pair is likely filling or nearly filling its Roche lobe, and they used

items.title: A Possible Non-Transiting Companion in the TOI-2109 System Supported by Transit Timing Variations
items.why: Finding hidden planets through gravity helps us map out entire solar systems.
items.summary: Astronomers studied a hot Jupiter planet for nearly twenty years to see how it orbits its star. They found evidence that a second, hidden planet is likely pulling on it with gravity.

items.title: ATel 18152: MAXI/GSC detection of an X-ray flare from GT Mus on 2026-11-09 UT
items.why: Observing X-ray flares helps scientists understand how much energy stars can release during sudden outbursts.
items.summary: A telescope detected a sudden burst of X-ray energy coming from a star called GT Mus. This flare was spotted by the MAXI/GSC instrument on November 9, 2026.

items.title: Simulated moon dust turned into LEGO-like blocks for settlements
items.why: Using local moon dust could make it much easier and cheaper to build habitats for future space travelers.
items.summary: Researchers have found a way to turn lunar dust, also known as regolith, into bricks that snap together like LEGO blocks. This material could be used with 3D printers to build permanent structures on the moon.

items.title: The Debris Disk Host β Piscis Austrinus is a Rapidly Rotating Star Seen Nearly Pole-On
items.why: This new method allows researchers to better understand the properties of stars that are viewed from the pole.
items.summary: Scientists used a new method to study a rapidly rotating star called beta Piscis Austrinus. They discovered that the star's poles are 24% hotter than its equator.

items.title: The Case for a Bubble at Life’s Start
items.why: Understanding how the first cells formed helps scientists know how life might begin elsewhere.
items.summary: Researchers are looking at the theory that life began inside a tiny bubble called a lipid membrane. This membrane would have provided a safe place for chemical reactions to create life.

items.title: Radial Velocity Confirmation of Two Binary Systems Detected with the Pulsation Timing Method
items.why: Confirming these binary systems helps scientists better understand the life cycles and compositions of different types of stars.
items.summary: Astronomers used telescope measurements to confirm that two specific star systems are actually pairs of stars orbiting one another. Both systems were found to contain a subdwarf B star and a white dwarf companion.

items.title: Detecting space objects with Earth-observation radar satellites
items.why: This method could provide a new way to track dangerous debris orbiting the Earth.
items.summary: Researchers tested if radar satellites used for observing Earth could also detect small pieces of space debris. They successfully identified various objects, including satellites and fragments, without needing prior orbital information.

items.title: The slower rotation of planet-hosting stars revisited
items.why: Understanding how star rotation relates to planet formation helps scientists learn how solar systems develop.
items.summary: Scientists looked at data from the Kepler and TESS missions to study how stars spin. They discovered that stars with planets around them tend to rotate more slowly than stars without planets.

items.title: ATel 18147: Spectroscopic Classification of Astrophysical Transients with the Lick Shane Telescope
items.why: Classifying these events helps scientists understand how different cosmic explosions work.
items.summary: Astronomers used the Shane telescope to look at the light from sudden, bright events in space. This helped them identify exactly what kind of objects these events were.

items.title: Newest Sample, Oldest Rock?
items.why: Comparing different rock samples helps scientists map out the geological history of Mars.
items.summary: The Perseverance rover has collected a new rock sample named Pumbe. This rock looks very similar to a rock found earlier called Badger Peak.

items.title: ATel 18145: Optical follow-up of a turn-on changing-look AGN AT2022aamy
items.why: Observing these changes helps scientists understand how active galaxies behave.
items.summary: Astronomers used a telescope to observe a changing-look active galactic nucleus called AT2022aamy. They looked at specific light patterns called emission lines.

items.title: The Sky Today on Wednesday, November 11: Venus comes to a halt
items.why: It marks the end of the moon's retrograde motion as it moves through the constellation Virgo.
items.summary: The moon of Saturn named Venus will appear to stop moving westward against the stars this week. This event happens at 10 A.M. EST on November 10.

items.title: APOD: 2026 November 11 – NGC 4449: Small Galaxy, Big Impact
items.why: It provides a visual way for the public to observe and learn about different types of galaxies.
items.summary: This is an astronomy picture of the small galaxy known as NGC 4449. It is part of NASA's daily archive of space images.

digest.text: Astronomers have identified a "runaway star" that is traveling at high speeds in an unusual direction. While most stars in our galaxy follow orderly, predictable paths, this specific star is deviating significantly from the standard movement of its neighbors. This discovery provides new insights into the chaotic forces that can eject stars from their typical orbits.

corrections.wrong: The new list of spacecraft around Earth described the Swift observatory as working. It re-entered the atmosphere on 4 November 2026, six days earlier.
corrections.effect: The Earth card of the public Solar System tab, for a few hours.
corrections.found: Swift had no current orbit data when the Earth-orbit view was being built.
corrections.fix: The entry now says what happened; spacecraft lists are checked against current orbit data.

corrections.wrong: In the new high-quality mode the map drew no galaxies, only its rings and labels.
corrections.effect: The public 3D map showed no galaxies for about 40 minutes.
corrections.found: Looking at the page after the update; the automatic tests have no graphics card, so they could not see it.
corrections.fix: Fixed, and the page test now reads the drawing code for this kind of mistake.

corrections.wrong: The first daily run placed no planet or spacecraft: NASA/JPL Horizons had stopped putting the numbers in the format the job asked for.
corrections.effect: Nothing public: the job refused to publish an empty map.
corrections.found: The job's own check (fewer than 10 objects means something is wrong).
corrections.fix: It reads Horizons' other format; all 46 objects were checked one by one against the live service.

corrections.wrong: When the VizieR catalogue service at Harvard was down, it sent tidy empty pages, and the software read them as "no known variable star here" and "no galaxies".
corrections.effect: 17 stars were briefly listed (privately) as possible new variable stars without a real catalogue check; the public 3D map was replaced by an empty file for a few minutes.
corrections.found: Suspiciously many candidates appeared, and the map stopped loading.
corrections.fix: An answer must now name the catalogue it came from, and a download must be nearly complete before it replaces anything. Local copies of the catalogues and a second working mirror were added, and the 17 stars were checked again.

corrections.wrong: Two neighbouring stars showed the same 6.4422-day period. TESS pixels are 21 arcseconds wide (an arcsecond is a tiny angle on the sky), so one star's light shows up in both.

papers.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
papers.authors: Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, Jason J. Wang, Katherine L. Bouman, William T. Freeman, Laurent Pueyo, Brandon Y. Feng, Marshall D. Perrin
papers.summary: Researchers developed a new way to subtract the bright glare of stars from images to reveal much fainter planets. By using a flexible physical model and a math technique called automatic differentiation, they successfully detected the planet 51 Eridani b using James Webb Space Telescope data.
papers.why: This method makes it much easier to see distant planets and helps prepare us for future missions that aim to image Earth-like worlds.

papers.title: A Possible Non-Transiting Companion in the TOI-2109 System Supported by Transit Timing Variations
papers.authors: Kaviya Parthasarathy, Prangsutip Cherdwongsung, Ing-Guey Jiang, Li-Chin Yeh, Hsin-Min Liu, Shraddha Biswas, D. Bisht, Napaporn A-thano et al.
papers.summary: Researchers studied a hot Jupiter planet called TOI-2109 b by looking at its transit timings over nearly twenty years. They found evidence that a second, hidden planet is likely tugging on the first one through gravity.
papers.why: This helps astronomers detect planets that don't pass directly in front of their star by watching how they mess up the timing of other planets.

papers.title: A TESS Disappearing Act: The Vanishing Transits of TOI-2535 b
papers.authors: Samuel W. Yee, Erik A. Petigura, Rafael Brahm, Karen A. Collins, Gregor Srdoc, David W. Latham, Allyson Bieryla, Victoria DiTomasso et al.
papers.summary: Astronomers used TESS data to find a hot Jupiter planet called TOI-2535 b that is actually moving out of our line of sight. Because of a nearby planet pulling on it, the planet's path across its star has shifted so much that its transits are disappearing.
papers.why: This is the first time scientists have directly watched a planet's transits vanish because its orbit changed due to interactions with another planet.

papers.title: Beyond the Fast Rotators: A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Substellar Weather
papers.authors: Natalia Oliveros-Gomez, Elena Manjavacas, Niall Whiteford, Caprice Phillips, Jared Bull, Kielan Hoch, Allison M. McCarthy, Beatriz Campos Estrada et al.
papers.summary: Researchers are proposing a large-scale study using the James Webb Space Telescope to look at the weather on brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets. Instead of looking at just one object at a time, they want to observe a wide variety of these objects to see how their clouds and temperatures change over time.
papers.why: This study will help scientists understand how atmospheric structures and weather patterns depend on things like how fast an object rotates and its physical properties.

papers.title: Tracing the Epoch of Reionization through extreme emission line galaxies around Cosmic Noon
papers.authors: M. Delgado Mancheño, J. Gallego, S. Pascual, M. Tang, R. Pello, N. Laporte, A. Camps-Fariña, M. Chamorro-Cazorla
papers.summary: Researchers studied a specific group of small, intense galaxies called Extreme Emission Line Galaxies (EELGs) located at a period called 'cosmic noon.' They found that these galaxies are compact, low-mass, and actively forming stars, which makes them good stand-ins for much older galaxies.
papers.why: Studying these closer galaxies helps scientists understand the much fainter galaxies that actually drove the reionization of the universe.

papers.title: Towards a new model of the compact triple system $λ$ Tauri I. Improved periods and preliminary elements of the triple system
papers.authors: P. Harmanec, J. Švrčková, P. Doležal, H. Božić, D. Vokrouhlický, P. Zasche, M. Šlechta, B. N. Barlow et al.
papers.summary: Researchers analyzed new and old data to create much more accurate timing models for the orbits in the triple star system λ Tauri. They found that one star in the inner pair is likely filling or nearly filling its Roche lobe, and they used the stability of the orbits to limit how much mass is being transferred between stars.
papers.why: Improving these orbital models helps scientists understand how complex star systems evolve and how stars interact with each other.

papers.title: Near-Ultraviolet and Optical Observations of the White Dwarf ZTF J0328$-$1219 Reveal Variable Periodicity in its Transiting Debris System
papers.authors: Joseph A. Guidry, J. J. Hermes, Zachary P. Vanderbosch, Boris Gaensicke, Simon Blouin, Laura K. Rogers, Jay Farihi, Stefan Arseneau et al.
papers.summary: Astronomers used the Hubble Space Telescope and other tools to watch a white dwarf star surrounded by a disk of debris. They found that the timing of the debris passing in front of the star is changing, suggesting that collisions are happening within the disk.
papers.why: This allows scientists to study how dust and debris behave in real time around a dying star.

papers.title: On the Detectability of Compact Multi-Planet Systems via Gravitational Microlensing
papers.summary: Researchers studied whether a group of planets orbiting a small star, like TRAPPIST-1, could be spotted using a technique called gravitational microlensing. They found that even when combining the signals of all seven planets, the effect is far too small to be detected by current or upcoming technology.
papers.why: This helps astronomers understand the limits of different methods for finding planets and shows that the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope won't be able to find these specific types of systems using microlensing.

papers.title: Latest $ν$s from the Earliest Galaxies: Probing neutrino self-interactions with JWST
papers.authors: Ranjini Mondol, Priyank Parashari, Anirban Das, Vera Gluscevic, Ranjan Laha
papers.summary: Researchers used new data from the James Webb Space Telescope and the Planck satellite to look for evidence of neutrinos interacting with themselves. They found that these observations can set stricter limits on how strongly neutrinos interact compared to using satellite data alone.
papers.why: This matters because studying the earliest galaxies helps scientists test new theories in particle physics that cannot be easily tested on Earth.

papers.title: Interferometric survey of stellar parameters. Reliable methodology for a direct measurement of the angular diameter in exoplanet host stars
papers.authors: H. Nowacki, D. Mourard, N. Ebrahimkutty, R. V. Ibañez Bustos, J. Jonák, M. Vrard, G. Schaefer, P. Berio et al.
papers.summary: Researchers used the CHARA Array to measure the size of stars that have planets orbiting them. They found a way to measure star radii with about 2% precision, which helps improve how accurately we know the size and mass of their planets.
papers.why: This matters because knowing the exact size and mass of a star is necessary to truly understand the planets orbiting them.
